title: The world had just shrunk — the 80-day loop
learning_goal: Know the three enablers of 1869–70 and the eight legs that add up to eighty; feel the thrill of the map lighting up.

narration.script: How could anyone even think it? Because the world had just shrunk. When one of the card players said the world was big, Fogg's answer was three words: 'It was once.' Look at the three lights. The Suez Canal, opened in November 1869. The American railroad, joined at Promontory Summit in May 1869. The last rail link across India, closed at Jabalpur in March 1870. Three doors, opened within ten months, two years before tonight. Now watch the line draw. London to Suez, by rail and steamer through Mont Cenis and Brindisi, seven days. Suez to Bombay by steamer, thirteen. Bombay to Calcutta by rail, three. Calcutta to Hong Kong, thirteen. Hong Kong to Yokohama, six. Yokohama to San Francisco, twenty-two. San Francisco to New York by rail, seven. New York back to London, nine. Add them up: eighty. Now tap the longest leg on the map.
narration.after_script: The Pacific — twenty-two days of ocean; keep this in mind for later. And the map fades back to tonight: only London lit. Because Fogg, still at the table, says the sentence that turns the evening. 'The train leaves for Dover at a quarter before nine.'

variants.clear: How could anyone believe this plan? Because the world had just become smaller. When one of the card players said the world was big, Fogg answered with three words: 'It was once.' Look at the three lights. The Suez Canal opened in 1869. The American railroad, coast to coast, was joined in 1869. The last rail link across India closed the gap in 1870. Three doors, all opened within ten months, two years before tonight. Now watch the line draw. London to Suez: seven days. Suez to Bombay, by ship: thirteen. Bombay to Calcutta, by rail: three. Calcutta to Hong Kong: thirteen. Hong Kong to Yokohama: six. Yokohama to San Francisco: twenty-two. San Francisco to New York, by rail: seven. New York back to London: nine. Add them up: eighty. Now tap the longest leg on the map.

interaction.prompt: Tap the longest leg of Fogg's route.

options.feedback: Rail and steamer, via Mont Cenis and Brindisi: 7 days.
Steamer across the Arabian Sea: 13 days. Long, but not the longest.
Rail across India — the newest link, only just opened: 3 days.
Steamer: 13 days. Same as Suez to Bombay.
The Pacific: 22 days by steamer — the longest leg by far. Keep this in mind for later.
Rail, coast to coast, possible only since May 1869: 7 days.

transition.out: hard cut to the packing game
transition.music_cue: M-41 swell from 30 s, out at 90 s under the turn line

production_notes: G-01 must deliver both the full-loop and the Day-1 layer plus the requested 'enablers' layer. Tap-to-find is interactive only; the eight legs are map targets (≥ 44 px), not a quiz; option feedback is text-only (never voiced — so the 'keep this in mind' tic is spoken once). Wait state: after 'Now tap the longest leg on the map' the guide pauses (pause_narration) until the tap or 20 s (timeout_s), then narration.after_script plays over the fade back to Day 1. Linear cut: 40 s — enablers + loop reveal + turn line, no tap; skip 09 before it. Narrator: put a short 40-s linear form of the legs beat here for A4. NARRATOR (A1) — 40-s LINEAR FORM of the legs beat (≈ 90 words, for A4; replaces script+after_script in the linear cut, no tap): "How could anyone even think it? Because the world had just shrunk — the Suez Canal, 1869; the American railroad, 1869; the last rail link across India, 1870. Three doors, opened within ten months. Now watch the line draw: seven days to Suez, thirteen to Bombay, three to Calcutta, thirteen to Hong Kong, six to Yokohama, twenty-two across the Pacific, seven across America, nine home. Eighty. And Fogg, still at the table, says the sentence that turns the evening: 'The train leaves for Dover at a quarter before nine.'"
